title: Der Trommler
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 193. Text from Wikisource („Der Trommler (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 193 starts from a small theft: a drummer walking by a lake at evening pockets one of three pieces of white linen lying on the shore, and that night a voice at his bed asks for her shift back — a king’s daughter in a witch’s power, held on a glass mountain, who cannot fly home without it. Getting to the mountain takes a bluff on the drum that persuades a giant an army is behind him, and a saddle that carries whoever sits in it wherever he wishes; getting her takes three days’ work no one could do — a pond bailed out with a thimble, a forest felled with a leaden axe — and the witch thrown into her own fire. Then the tale turns a second time, on a kiss he was told not to give: he greets his parents on the right cheek, forgets her entirely, and her rhymed call — “Trommler, Trommler, hör mich an” — has to be made outside his bedroom door on three successive nights before it reaches him.

sentences.t: Eines Abends gieng ein junger Trommler ganz allein auf dem Feld und kam an einen See, da sah er an dem Ufer drei Stückchen weiße Leinewand liegen.
sentences.l: One evening a young drummer went quite alone on the field and came to a lake, there he saw on the bank three little pieces of white linen cloth lying.
sentences.i: One evening a young drummer was walking quite alone across the fields and came to a lake, where he saw three little pieces of white linen lying on the bank.
sentences.n: “einen See” is der See, masculine — the lake. Feminine die See would be the sea, and this whole opening happens on a lakeshore. “eines Abends” is a genitive of time: of an evening, that is, one evening. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: „Was für feines Leinen“ sprach er, und steckte eins davon in die Tasche.
sentences.l: “What fine linen” said he, and put one of them into his pocket.
sentences.i: “What fine linen,” he said, and slipped one of the pieces into his pocket.
sentences.n: “was für” = what sort of, used here as a bare exclamation with no verb. “eins” is neuter, standing for one of the Stückchen. The 1857 printing closes the quotation without a comma before the speech tag, which is its normal habit.

sentences.t: Er gieng heim, dachte nicht weiter an seinen Fund und legte sich zu Bett.
sentences.l: He went home, thought no further about his find, and laid himself to bed.
sentences.i: He went home, thought no more about what he had found, and went to bed.
sentences.n: der Fund is the noun — a find, the thing found — from finden. “legte sich zu Bett” is the old fixed phrase for going to bed; modern German says ins Bett gehen.

sentences.t: Als er eben einschlafen wollte, war es ihm als nennte jemand seinen Namen.
sentences.l: When he was just about to fall asleep, it was to him as though someone were speaking his name.
sentences.i: Just as he was about to fall asleep, it seemed to him that someone was calling his name.
sentences.n: “es war ihm als …” = it seemed to him as if. The subjunctive “nennte” marks the whole thing as an impression rather than a fact — German uses the verb form where English would add “seemed”.

sentences.t: Er horchte und vernahm eine leise Stimme, die ihm zurief „Trommeler, Trommeler, wach auf.“
sentences.l: He hearkened and heard a soft voice, which called to him “Drummer, drummer, wake up.”
sentences.i: He listened, and made out a soft voice calling to him “Drummer, drummer, wake up.”
sentences.n: “Trommeler”, with the extra e, is the spelling the 1857 printing uses in this one call, where it stands twice over; everywhere else the tale writes Trommler. vernehmen is the elevated verb for hearing or perceiving. aufwachen is separable: wach auf.

sentences.t: Er konnte, da es finstere Nacht war, niemand sehen, aber es kam ihm vor als schwebte eine Gestalt vor seinem Bett auf und ab.
sentences.l: He could, since it was pitch-dark night, see nobody, but it came to him as though a shape were hovering up and down before his bed.
sentences.i: He could see nobody, for it was pitch-dark night, but it seemed to him that a shape was hovering up and down before his bed.
sentences.n: “da” at the head of a clause means since, because — not “there”. vorkommen is separable: kam … vor, to seem. The subjunctive “schwebte” again keeps it an impression.

sentences.t: „Was willst du?“ fragte er.
sentences.l: “What do you want?” he asked.
sentences.n: du is rendered “you” throughout — the drummer and the voice speak to each other directly and informally, and no archaic pronoun is needed to carry that.

sentences.t: „Gib mir mein Hemdchen zurück,“ antwortete die Stimme, „das du mir gestern Abend am See weggenommen hast.“
sentences.l: “Give me back my little shirt,” answered the voice, “that you took away from me yesterday evening at the lake.”
sentences.i: “Give me back my little shirt,” the voice answered, “the one you took from me yesterday evening at the lake.”
sentences.n: zurückgeben is separable — gib … zurück, with the particle at the end. The relative clause belonging to Hemdchen has been held back until after the speech tag. The dative “mir” names the person robbed: took it from me.

sentences.t: „Du sollst es wieder haben,“ sprach der Trommler, „wenn du mir sagst wer du bist.“
sentences.l: “You shall have it again,” said the drummer, “if you tell me who you are.”
sentences.n: “sprach” is this tale’s ordinary word for “said” — the plain past of sprechen, not a raised register in German even though it looks formal to an English eye.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ erwiederte die Stimme, „ich bin die Tochter eines mächtigen Königs, aber ich bin in die Gewalt einer Hexe gerathen, und bin auf den Glasberg gebannt.
sentences.l: “Ah,” replied the voice, “I am the daughter of a mighty king, but I have fallen into the power of a witch, and am spellbound to the glass mountain.
sentences.i: “Ah,” the voice replied, “I am the daughter of a mighty king, but I have fallen into a witch’s power, and am held by a spell on the glass mountain.
sentences.n: “erwiederte” is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte. geraten (here “gerathen”, with the old th) means to get into something without intending to. bannen is to bind by a spell: she is fixed to the mountain, not merely living there.

sentences.t: Jeden Tag muß ich mich mit meinen zwei Schwestern im See baden, aber ohne mein Hemdchen kann ich nicht wieder fort fliegen.
sentences.l: Every day I must bathe myself with my two sisters in the lake, but without my little shirt I cannot fly away again.
sentences.i: Every day I must bathe in the lake with my two sisters, but without my little shirt I cannot fly away again.
sentences.n: The shirt is what makes them swan-maidens. The tale never says so; it simply lets the flying stand as a fact and leaves the reader to see the shape of the older story behind it. “fort fliegen” is printed as two words in 1857 where modern German has fortfliegen.

sentences.t: Meine Schwestern haben sich fort gemacht, ich aber habe zurück bleiben müssen.
sentences.l: My sisters have made themselves off, but I have had to stay behind.
sentences.i: My sisters got away, but I have had to stay behind.
sentences.n: “sich fort machen” = to make off. “habe … bleiben müssen” is the double infinitive: where English says “have had to stay”, German leaves müssen in the infinitive at the end instead of using a past participle.

sentences.t: Ich bitte dich gib mir mein Hemdchen wieder.“
sentences.l: I beg you, give me my little shirt back.
sentences.n: Two clauses run straight together without a comma, as the 1857 printing often does — “ich bitte dich” and then the plain imperative “gib”.

sentences.t: „Sei ruhig, armes Kind,“ sprach der Trommler, „ich will dirs gerne zurückgeben.“
sentences.l: “Be calm, poor child,” said the drummer, “I will gladly give it back to you.”
sentences.i: “Be easy, poor child,” said the drummer, “I will gladly give it back to you.”
sentences.n: “dirs” is dir + es run together: to you it. “will” is not a future here but the older full sense of wollen — I am willing, I mean to.

sentences.t: Er holte es aus seiner Tasche, und reichte es ihr in der Dunkelheit hin.
sentences.l: He fetched it out of his pocket, and held it out to her in the darkness.
sentences.n: hinreichen is separable, and its particle “hin” has travelled to the very end of the clause — the shape to watch for whenever a German sentence seems to end on a stray little word.

sentences.t: Sie erfaßte es hastig, und wollte damit fort.
sentences.l: She seized it hastily, and wanted away with it.
sentences.i: She snatched it up hastily and made to be off with it.
sentences.n: “wollte damit fort” has no verb of motion at all: wollen carries the sentence alone and the reader supplies “go”. The ellipsis is very common with fort, weg and hinaus.

sentences.t: „Weile einen Augenblick,“ sagte er „vielleicht kann ich dir helfen.“
sentences.l: “Tarry a moment,” said he “perhaps I can help you.”
sentences.i: “Wait a moment,” he said, “perhaps I can help you.”
sentences.n: weilen is the elevated old verb for lingering; the everyday word would be warten. The 1857 printing sets no comma after “sagte er”.

sentences.t: „Helfen kannst du mir nur, wenn du auf den Glasberg steigst und mich aus der Gewalt der Hexe befreist.
sentences.l: “Help me you can only if you climb up the glass mountain and free me out of the power of the witch.
sentences.i: “You can only help me if you climb the glass mountain and free me from the witch’s power.
sentences.n: The infinitive “Helfen” is thrown to the front for emphasis, which drives the finite verb “kannst” into second place and the subject after it. English cannot copy that without sounding broken, so the idiomatic line restores the order.

sentences.t: Aber zu dem Glasberg kommst du nicht, und wenn du auch ganz nahe daran wärst, so kannst du nicht hinauf.“
sentences.l: But to the glass mountain you do not come, and even if you were quite close to it, you cannot get up.”
sentences.i: But you will never reach the glass mountain; and even if you stood right at its foot, you could not get up it.”
sentences.n: “und wenn … auch” = even if. “so kannst du nicht hinauf” has no verb of motion either — hinauf, upward, carries the whole thought.

sentences.t: „Was ich will, das kann ich,“ sagte der Trommler, „ich habe Mitleid mit dir und ich fürchte mich vor nichts.
sentences.l: “What I will, that I can,” said the drummer, “I have pity with you and I fear myself before nothing.
sentences.i: “What I set my mind on, I can do,” said the drummer; “I pity you, and I am afraid of nothing.
sentences.n: “Was ich will, das kann ich” puts the object clause first and then picks it up again with “das” — a resumptive pronoun German uses constantly and English drops. sich fürchten vor + dative is the standard frame for being afraid of something.

sentences.t: Aber ich weiß den Weg nicht, der nach dem Glasberge führt.“
sentences.l: But I do not know the way that leads to the glass mountain.”
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb wissen — I know — and not the adjective weiß, white, which the same spelling also carries. “Glasberge” carries the old dative ‑e after nach, which 1857 German still uses freely and modern German has all but dropped.

sentences.t: „Der Weg geht durch den großen Wald, in dem die Menschenfresser hausen,“ antwortete sie, „mehr darf ich dir nicht sagen.“
sentences.l: “The way goes through the great forest, in which the man-eaters house,” she answered, “more I may not tell you.”
sentences.i: “The road goes through the great forest, where the man-eaters have their haunt,” she answered; “more than that I may not tell you.”
sentences.n: hausen is a menacing verb — to dwell in the sense of to infest, to hold sway. “darf” is dürfen, to be permitted: she is not unwilling but forbidden. The Menschenfresser turn out in the next block to be giants, and the tale never pauses to reconcile the two words.

sentences.t: Darauf hörte er wie sie fortschwirrte.
sentences.l: Thereupon he heard how she whirred away.
sentences.i: Thereupon he heard her whirring off.
sentences.n: “hörte … wie” is the ordinary German way of reporting something perceived — heard how she did it — where English uses a bare participle. fortschwirren is the sound of wings, and is the first plain sign that she flies.

sentences.t: Bei Anbruch des Tags machte sich der Trommler auf, hieng seine Trommel um und gieng ohne Furcht geradezu in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: At break of day the drummer set himself off, hung his drum about him and went without fear straight into the forest.
sentences.i: At daybreak the drummer set out, slung his drum about him and walked without fear straight into the forest.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs in one sentence: sich aufmachen (machte sich auf, to set out), umhängen (hieng … um, to sling round) and hineingehen (gieng … hinein). “hieng” is the 1857 spelling of hing.

sentences.t: Als er ein Weilchen gegangen war und keinen Riesen erblickte, so dachte er „ich muß die Langeschläfer aufwecken,“ hieng die Trommel vor und schlug einen Wirbel, daß die Vögel aus den Bäumen mit Geschrei aufflogen.
sentences.l: When he had gone a little while and caught sight of no giant, he thought “I must wake the long-sleepers,” hung the drum in front and beat a roll, so that the birds flew up out of the trees with a great outcry.
sentences.i: When he had walked a little while and had caught sight of no giant, he thought “I must wake the lie-abeds,” swung the drum round to the front and beat a roll, so that the birds went up out of the trees with a great outcry.
sentences.n: einen Wirbel schlagen is to beat a drum roll — der Wirbel here is the roll, not the crown of the head. “daß” after a main clause often means so that, marking the result. Langeschläfer is a made-up compound of lang and Schläfer, sleeper — the drummer’s contemptuous name for the giants.

sentences.t: Nicht lange so erhob sich auch ein Riese in die Höhe, der im Gras gelegen und geschlafen hatte, und war so groß wie eine Tanne.
sentences.l: Not long, and a giant too raised himself up into the height, who had lain in the grass and slept, and was as big as a fir tree.
sentences.i: Before long a giant did rise up, who had been lying asleep in the grass, and he was as tall as a fir tree.
sentences.n: “nicht lange so …” is an old clipped construction — it was not long before. sich erheben, to rise up, is reflexive. The relative clause is left dangling behind the verb, and the whole giant is described only after he has already stood up.

sentences.t: „Du Wicht,“ rief er ihm zu, „was trommelst du hier und weckst mich aus dem besten Schlaf?“
sentences.l: “You wretch,” he called to him, “what are you drumming here for, and waking me out of my best sleep?”
sentences.i: “You wretch,” he shouted at him, “what are you drumming here for, waking me out of my soundest sleep?”
sentences.n: zurufen is separable: rief … zu, to call out to someone, with the person in the dative. “was trommelst du” is “what are you drumming for”, an idiomatic why rather than a literal what.

sentences.t: „Ich trommle,“ antwortete er, „weil viele tausende hinter mir herkommen, damit sie den Weg wissen.“
sentences.l: “I am drumming,” he answered, “because many thousands are coming along behind me, so that they may know the way.”
sentences.n: “damit” introduces a purpose clause — so that. “die” before Weg is not a demonstrative here; “den Weg wissen” is simply to know the road. The drummer is lying, and the whole scene turns on the giant believing him.

sentences.t: „Was wollen die hier in meinem Wald?“ fragte der Riese.
sentences.l: “What do they want here in my forest?” asked the giant.
sentences.n: “die” stands alone as a demonstrative pronoun: those ones, them. German uses der/die/das this way in speech far more freely than English uses “those”.

sentences.t: „Sie wollen dir den Garaus machen und den Wald von einem Ungethüm, wie du bist, säubern.“
sentences.l: “They want to finish you off and cleanse the forest of a monster such as you are.”
sentences.i: “They mean to make an end of you and to rid the forest of a brute like you.”
sentences.n: “den Garaus machen” is a fixed idiom — to make an end of someone. “Ungethüm” is the 1857 spelling of Ungetüm, a monstrous brute. “wie du bist” is literally “as you are”, where English says “like you”.

sentences.t: „Oho,“ sagte der Riese, „ich trete euch wie Ameisen todt.“
sentences.l: “Oho,” said the giant, “I tread you dead like ants.”
sentences.i: “Oho,” said the giant, “I will tread you flat like ants.”
sentences.n: “todt” is the 1857 spelling of tot. todt treten — to tread dead — is the ordinary German way of saying to trample something to death, and the present tense here does duty for a threat about the future.

sentences.t: „Meinst du, du könntest gegen sie etwas ausrichten?“ sprach der Trommler, „wenn du dich bückst, um einen zu packen, so springt er fort und versteckt sich:
sentences.l: “Do you think you could accomplish anything against them?” said the drummer, “if you stoop down to grab one, then he springs away and hides himself:
sentences.i: “Do you suppose you could do anything against them?” said the drummer. “If you stoop to seize one, he springs off and hides:
sentences.n: “könntest” is subjunctive — could, in a hypothetical. ausrichten is to get something done, to accomplish. “um … zu packen” is the purpose infinitive: in order to seize.

sentences.t: wie du dich aber niederlegst und schläfst, so kommen sie aus allen Gebüschen herbei, und kriechen an dir hinauf.
sentences.l: but as you lie yourself down and sleep, then they come up out of all the bushes, and creep up you.
sentences.i: but the moment you lie down and sleep, they come out of every bush and creep up you.
sentences.n: “wie” again introduces time — as, the moment that. niederlegen is separable and reflexive: legst … nieder. “an dir hinauf” — up along you — puts two little directional words together, which German does readily.

sentences.t: Jeder hat einen Hammer von Stahl am Gürtel stecken, damit schlagen sie dir den Schädel ein.“
sentences.l: Each has a hammer of steel stuck at his belt, with that they beat your skull in.”
sentences.i: Each of them has a steel hammer stuck in his belt, and with that they beat your skull in.”
sentences.n: “von Stahl” = of steel; Stahl is the metal, not a form of stehlen, to steal. “stecken” after haben is a bare infinitive standing where English would use a participle: has it stuck there. einschlagen is separable — schlagen … ein. The dative “dir” is the possessive: your skull.

sentences.t: Der Riese ward verdrießlich und dachte „wenn ich mich mit dem listigen Volk befasse, so könnte es doch zu meinem Schaden ausschlagen.
sentences.l: The giant became sullen and thought “if I meddle with the cunning folk, it could turn out to my harm after all.
sentences.i: The giant grew sullen and thought “if I get mixed up with this cunning folk, it might well end badly for me.
sentences.n: “ward” is the archaic past of werden, modern wurde. sich befassen mit is to concern oneself with, to meddle with. ausschlagen here means to turn out a certain way. “das Volk” is High German for folk, people — a collective, and used contemptuously.

sentences.t: Wölfen und Bären drücke ich die Gurgel zusammen, aber vor den Erdwürmen kann ich mich nicht schützen.“
sentences.l: Wolves and bears I press the throat together, but against the earth-worms I cannot protect myself.”
sentences.i: Wolves and bears I can throttle, but against these earthworms there is no protecting myself.”
sentences.n: “Wölfen und Bären drücke ich die Gurgel zusammen” is the dative of possession: I press the throat of wolves and bears together, that is, I throttle them. English needs a possessive where German uses the plain dative. Erdwürmen — earthworms — is the giant’s answer to the drummer’s ants.

sentences.t: „Hör, kleiner Kerl,“ sprach er, „zieh wieder ab, ich verspreche dir, daß ich dich und deine Gesellen in Zukunft in Ruhe lassen will,
sentences.l: “Hear, little fellow,” said he, “draw off again, I promise you that I will leave you and your companions in peace in future,
sentences.i: “Listen, little fellow,” said he, “be off with you; I promise you that I shall leave you and your fellows in peace from now on,
sentences.n: abziehen is separable: zieh … ab, to withdraw, march off. “in Ruhe lassen” is the fixed phrase for leaving someone alone. “in Zukunft” = in future, henceforth.

sentences.t: und hast du noch einen Wunsch, so sags mir, ich will dir wohl etwas zu Gefallen thun.“
sentences.l: and if you have still a wish, then say it to me, I will gladly do you some favour.”
sentences.i: and if you have any wish left, tell it to me; I am willing to do you a good turn.”
sentences.n: “hast du noch einen Wunsch” has no wenn — German can mark a conditional simply by putting the verb first, and the “so” that follows answers it. “sags” is sag + es run together. “etwas zu Gefallen thun” = to do someone a favour; das Gefallen here is the noun, not the verb gefallen, to please.

sentences.t: „Du hast lange Beine,“ sprach der Trommler, „und kannst schneller laufen als ich,
sentences.l: “You have long legs,” said the drummer, “and can run faster than I,
sentences.n: German compares with als where English uses “than”, and leaves the pronoun in the nominative — “als ich”, than I.

sentences.t: trag mich zum Glasberge, so will ich den Meinigen ein Zeichen zum Rückzug geben, und sie sollen dich diesmal in Ruhe lassen.“
sentences.l: carry me to the glass mountain, and I will give my people a sign for the retreat, and they shall leave you in peace this time.”
sentences.i: carry me to the glass mountain, and I will give my people the signal to withdraw, and they shall leave you alone this time.”
sentences.n: “die Meinigen” — the mine ones — is a substantivized possessive meaning my own people. There are of course no people; the drummer is still spinning the same lie.

sentences.t: „Komm her, Wurm,“ sprach der Riese, „setz dich auf meine Schulter, ich will dich tragen wohin du verlangst.“
sentences.l: “Come here, worm,” said the giant, “set yourself on my shoulder, I will carry you wherever you ask.”
sentences.i: “Come here, worm,” said the giant, “sit on my shoulder, and I will carry you wherever you please.”
sentences.n: sich setzen is reflexive — to seat oneself. verlangen is to demand or ask for; “wohin du verlangst” = wherever you ask to go, with the verb of motion again left out.

sentences.t: Der Riese hob ihn hinauf, und der Trommler fieng oben an nach Herzenslust auf der Trommel zu wirbeln.
sentences.l: The giant lifted him up, and the drummer began up there to whirl on the drum to his heart’s content.
sentences.i: The giant lifted him up, and up there the drummer began to beat rolls on his drum to his heart’s content.
sentences.n: anfangen is separable and its two halves stand far apart here: fieng … an. “nach Herzenslust” = to one’s heart’s content, a set phrase. wirbeln is what a drummer does — to beat a roll.

sentences.t: Der Riese dachte „das wird das Zeichen sein, daß das andere Volk zurückgehen soll.“
sentences.l: The giant thought “that will be the sign that the other folk shall go back.”
sentences.i: The giant thought “that will be the signal for the rest of them to turn back.”
sentences.n: “das wird … sein” is not a future but a guess about the present — that must be, that will be. German uses werden this way constantly.

sentences.t: Nach einer Weile stand ein zweiter Riese am Weg, der nahm den Trommler dem ersten ab und steckte ihn in sein Knopfloch.
sentences.l: After a while a second giant stood on the way, he took the drummer from the first and stuck him into his buttonhole.
sentences.i: After a while a second giant was standing by the road; he took the drummer over from the first and stuck him into his buttonhole.
sentences.n: “der” at the head of the second clause is a demonstrative pronoun, not a relative — he, that one. abnehmen is separable and takes the dative of the person relieved: nahm … dem ersten ab, took him off the first one.

sentences.t: Der Trommler faßte den Knopf, der wie eine Schüssel groß war, hielt sich daran und schaute ganz lustig umher.
sentences.l: The drummer grasped the button, which was as big as a bowl, held on to it and looked about him quite merrily.
sentences.i: The drummer took hold of the button, which was as big as a bowl, held fast to it and looked cheerfully about him.
sentences.n: “hielt sich daran” — held himself to it; da(r)- plus a preposition is German’s way of saying “to it, on it, by it” for things rather than people. The tale gives the giant’s scale only through such details.

sentences.t: Dann kamen sie zu einem dritten, der nahm ihn aus dem Knopfloch und setzte ihn auf den Rand seines Hutes;
sentences.l: Then they came to a third, he took him out of the buttonhole and set him on the brim of his hat;
sentences.i: Then they came to a third, who took him out of the buttonhole and set him on the brim of his hat;
sentences.n: Three giants in three sentences, with nothing said about who they are or why they pass him along. The 1857 text simply does not make the connection, and the apparatus does not supply one.

sentences.t: da gieng der Trommler oben auf und ab und sah über die Bäume hinaus,
sentences.l: there the drummer walked up and down on top and looked out over the trees,
sentences.i: up there the drummer walked to and fro and looked out over the trees,
sentences.n: “auf und ab” = up and down, to and fro. “hinaus” marks the direction of the looking: out and away from where he stands.

sentences.t: und als er in blauer Ferne einen Berg erblickte, so dachte er „das ist gewis der Glasberg,“ und er war es auch.
sentences.l: and when he caught sight of a mountain in the blue distance, he thought “that is surely the glass mountain,” and so it was.
sentences.i: and when he caught sight of a mountain in the blue distance, he thought “that must be the glass mountain” — and so it was.
sentences.n: “gewis” is the 1857 spelling of gewiß. “und er war es auch” — and it was it too — is the narrator confirming the guess, a small aside of a kind this tale uses sparingly.

sentences.t: Der Riese that nur noch ein paar Schritte, so waren sie an dem Fuß des Bergs angelangt, wo ihn der Riese absetzte.
sentences.l: The giant took only a few more steps, and they had arrived at the foot of the mountain, where the giant set him down.
sentences.i: The giant took only a few more strides, and they were at the foot of the mountain, where he set the drummer down.
sentences.n: “so waren sie …” — the so answers the first clause and means and then, whereupon. absetzen is separable: setzte … ab, to set down.

sentences.t: Der Trommler verlangte er sollte ihn auch auf die Spitze des Glasberges tragen, aber der Riese schüttelte mit dem Kopf, brummte etwas in den Bart und gieng in den Wald zurück.
sentences.l: The drummer demanded he should carry him to the summit of the glass mountain too, but the giant shook his head, grumbled something into his beard and went back into the forest.
sentences.i: The drummer demanded that he should carry him to the summit of the glass mountain as well, but the giant shook his head, muttered something into his beard and went back into the forest.
sentences.n: “verlangte er sollte” has no daß at all — German can drop the conjunction and mark reported speech with the subjunctive “sollte” alone. “schüttelte mit dem Kopf” takes mit where modern German usually says den Kopf schütteln. “etwas in den Bart brummen” is the same picture as English muttering into one’s beard.

sentences.t: Nun stand der arme Trommler vor dem Berg, der so hoch war, als wenn drei Berge aufeinander gesetzt wären, und dabei so glatt wie ein Spiegel,
sentences.l: Now the poor drummer stood before the mountain, which was so high as if three mountains had been set one upon another, and withal as smooth as a mirror,
sentences.i: Now the poor drummer stood before the mountain, which was as high as if three mountains had been set one on top of another, and smooth as a mirror besides,
sentences.n: “als wenn … wären” is the subjunctive of comparison — as if. “dabei” here means with that, into the bargain, and is rendered “withal” in the literal line only to keep its position visible.

sentences.t: und wußte keinen Rath um hinauf zu kommen.
sentences.l: and knew no counsel for getting up.
sentences.i: and could think of no way of getting up it.
sentences.n: “keinen Rath wissen” is the fixed phrase for being at a loss — to know no remedy. “Rath” is the 1857 spelling of Rat.

sentences.t: Er fieng an zu klettern, aber vergeblich, er rutschte immer wieder herab.
sentences.l: He began to climb, but in vain, he slid down again and again.
sentences.n: anfangen is separable: fieng … an. “immer wieder” = again and again, over and over.

sentences.t: „Wer jetzt ein Vogel wäre“ dachte er, aber was half das Wünschen, es wuchsen ihm keine Flügel.
sentences.l: “Whoever were a bird now” he thought, but what did the wishing help, no wings grew on him.
sentences.i: “If only one were a bird now,” he thought — but what use was wishing? no wings grew on him.
sentences.n: “Wer jetzt ein Vogel wäre” is a wish left hanging, with the subjunctive “wäre” doing all the work and no main clause at all. “es wuchsen ihm keine Flügel” is the dative of possession again: no wings grew to him, that is, he grew none.

sentences.t: Indem er so stand, und sich nicht zu helfen wußte, erblickte er nicht weit von sich zwei Männer, die heftig miteinander stritten.
sentences.l: While he stood so, and did not know how to help himself, he caught sight not far from him of two men who were quarrelling violently with each other.
sentences.i: As he stood there, at a loss what to do, he caught sight of two men not far off, quarrelling violently with one another.
sentences.n: “indem” at the head of a clause means while, in the course of. “sich nicht zu helfen wissen” = not to know what to do with oneself, to be helpless — it recurs later in the tale.

sentences.t: Er gieng auf sie zu und sah daß sie wegen eines Sattels uneins waren, der vor ihnen auf der Erde lag und den jeder von ihnen haben wollte.
sentences.l: He went up to them and saw that they were at odds over a saddle, which lay before them on the ground and which each of them wanted to have.
sentences.i: He went up to them and saw that they were at odds over a saddle that lay on the ground before them and that each of them wanted for himself.
sentences.n: zugehen auf is separable: gieng … zu, to walk up to. “wegen eines Sattels” takes the genitive. This is der Sattel, the riding saddle, and its magic is explained in a moment.

sentences.t: „Was seid ihr für Narren,“ sprach er, „zankt euch um einen Sattel und habt kein Pferd dazu.“
sentences.l: “What fools you are,” said he, “you squabble over a saddle and have no horse to go with it.”
sentences.i: “What fools you are,” said he; “squabbling over a saddle, and no horse to put it on.”
sentences.n: “was seid ihr für Narren” — what for fools are you — is the was für construction again, here in a full sentence. sich zanken um is to quarrel over. “dazu” = to go with it, belonging to it.

sentences.t: „Der Sattel ist werth daß man darum streitet,“ antwortete der eine von den Männern,
sentences.l: “The saddle is worth that one quarrels about it,” answered the one of the men,
sentences.i: “The saddle is worth quarrelling over,” answered one of the two men,
sentences.n: “werth daß …” takes a full clause where English prefers a bare gerund: worth that one quarrels, worth quarrelling. “werth” is the 1857 spelling of wert.

sentences.t: „wer darauf sitzt und wünscht sich irgend wohin, und wärs am Ende der Welt, der ist im Augenblick angelangt, wie er den Wunsch ausgesprochen hat.
sentences.l: “whoever sits on it and wishes himself anywhere at all, and were it at the end of the world, he has arrived in the instant, as he has spoken the wish.
sentences.i: “whoever sits on it and wishes himself away anywhere at all — were it to the end of the world — is there the instant the wish is out of his mouth.
sentences.n: “und wärs am Ende der Welt” is und wäre es contracted, a subjunctive aside meaning even if it were. “der” picks up the whole “wer …” clause: he, that one — the resumptive pronoun German needs and English does without. “wie” once more means as, the moment that.

sentences.t: Der Sattel gehört uns gemeinschaftlich, die Reihe darauf zu reiten ist an mir, aber der andere will es nicht zulassen.“
sentences.l: The saddle belongs to us in common, the turn to ride on it is at me, but the other will not allow it.”
sentences.i: The saddle belongs to the two of us in common; it is my turn to ride on it, but the other will not have it so.”
sentences.n: “die Reihe ist an mir” is the fixed phrase for whose turn it is — die Reihe here is a turn, not a row. zulassen is separable and means to permit.

sentences.t: „Den Streit will ich bald austragen,“ sagte der Trommler, gieng eine Strecke weit und steckte einen weißen Stab in die Erde.
sentences.l: “The quarrel I will soon settle,” said the drummer, went a stretch away and stuck a white staff into the ground.
sentences.i: “I shall soon settle the quarrel,” said the drummer; he walked off some way and stuck a white staff into the ground.
sentences.n: austragen — literally to carry out — means to settle or fight out a dispute. The object “Den Streit” stands first for emphasis, pushing the verb into second place, which English cannot copy comfortably.

sentences.t: Dann kam er zurück und sprach „jetzt lauft nach dem Ziel, wer zuerst dort ist, der reitet zuerst.“
sentences.l: Then he came back and said “now run to the mark, whoever is there first, he rides first.”
sentences.i: Then he came back and said “now run for the mark; whoever gets there first rides first.”
sentences.n: “lauft” is the plural imperative — run, both of you — not the third person “runs”. “wer … der …” is the same wer/der pairing as before: whoever …, he …

sentences.t: Beide setzten sich in Trab, aber kaum waren sie ein paar Schritte weg,
sentences.l: Both set themselves into a trot, but scarcely were they a few steps away,
sentences.i: Both set off at a trot, but they were scarcely a few paces off
sentences.n: “kaum waren sie …” with the verb first is the German inversion after kaum — scarcely had they. The “so” that opens the next sense-unit is what answers it.

sentences.t: so schwang sich der Trommler auf den Sattel, wünschte sich auf den Glasberg, und ehe man die Hand umdrehte, war er dort.
sentences.l: then the drummer swung himself onto the saddle, wished himself onto the glass mountain, and before one could turn one’s hand, he was there.
sentences.i: when the drummer swung himself into the saddle, wished himself onto the glass mountain, and before you could turn your hand over he was there.
sentences.n: “ehe man die Hand umdrehte” is the German equivalent of “before you could turn round” — an idiom for instantaneously. The drummer settles the quarrel by cheating both men, and the tale passes no judgment on it.

sentences.t: Auf dem Berg oben war eine Ebne, da stand ein altes steinernes Haus,
sentences.l: Up on the mountain there was a level plain, there stood an old stone house,
sentences.i: Up on the mountain there was a level plain, and on it stood an old house of stone,
sentences.n: “Ebne” is the 1857 spelling of Ebene, a plain or flat. “steinernes” is the adjective from der Stein — built of stone.

sentences.t: und vor dem Haus lag ein großer Fischteich, dahinter aber ein finsterer Wald.
sentences.l: and before the house lay a great fish-pond, but behind it a dark forest.
sentences.i: and before the house lay a great fish-pond, and behind that a dark forest.
sentences.n: “aber” in the second half is not an objection but a mere connective — and on the other hand. finster is darker and more forbidding than dunkel: gloomy, murky.

sentences.t: Menschen und Thiere sah er nicht, es war alles still,
sentences.l: People and animals he did not see, all was still,
sentences.i: Of people and animals he saw none; everything was still,
sentences.n: The objects “Menschen und Thiere” come first and the verb second, which is the ordinary German way of foregrounding — English has to reorder. “Thiere” is the 1857 spelling of Tiere.

sentences.t: nur der Wind raschelte in den Bäumen, und die Wolken zogen ganz nah über seinem Haupt weg.
sentences.l: only the wind rustled in the trees, and the clouds drew away quite close over his head.
sentences.i: only the wind rustled in the trees, and the clouds went by very close above his head.
sentences.n: wegziehen is separable: zogen … weg. “Haupt” is the elevated word for head, kept for high or solemn contexts; the everyday word is Kopf, which this tale also uses. Wolken here is plain High German for clouds.

sentences.t: Er trat an die Thüre und klopfte an.
sentences.l: He stepped up to the door and knocked.
sentences.n: anklopfen is separable: klopfte … an. “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: Als er zum drittenmal geklopft hatte, öffnete eine Alte mit braunem Gesicht und rothen Augen die Thüre;
sentences.l: When he had knocked for the third time, an old woman with a brown face and red eyes opened the door;
sentences.i: When he had knocked a third time, an old woman with a brown face and red eyes opened the door;
sentences.n: “eine Alte” is an adjective used as a noun — an old one, an old woman. She is never given a name; the tale calls her die Alte throughout and only later die Hexe. “rothen” is the 1857 spelling of roten.

sentences.t: sie hatte eine Brille auf ihrer langen Nase und sah ihn scharf an, dann fragte sie was sein Begehren wäre.
sentences.l: she had spectacles on her long nose and looked at him keenly, then she asked what his desire might be.
sentences.i: she had spectacles on her long nose and looked him over sharply, then asked what he wanted.
sentences.n: ansehen is separable: sah … an. “was sein Begehren wäre” uses the subjunctive because it is reported speech — what his desire was, as she asked it. das Begehren is a noun made straight from the verb begehren, to desire.

sentences.t: „Einlaß, Kost und Nachtlager“ antwortete der Trommler.
sentences.l: “Admittance, food and a night’s lodging” answered the drummer.
sentences.i: “Admittance, board and a bed for the night,” answered the drummer.
sentences.n: Three bare nouns and no verb — the drummer answers as a traveller would at any door. “Einlaß” is the 1857 spelling of Einlass.

sentences.t: „Das sollst du haben,“ sagte die Alte, „wenn du dafür drei Arbeiten verrichten willst.“
sentences.l: “That you shall have,” said the old woman, “if you will perform three pieces of work for it.”
sentences.i: “That you shall have,” said the old woman, “if you will do three pieces of work in return.”
sentences.n: “dafür” = for that, in return for it. verrichten is a slightly formal verb for carrying out a task. Three tasks set by a witch is the shape the rest of this block follows.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht?“ antwortete er, „ich scheue keine Arbeit, und wenn sie noch so schwer ist.“
sentences.l: “Why not?” answered he, “I shrink from no work, and be it ever so hard.”
sentences.i: “Why not?” he answered. “I shrink from no work, however hard it may be.”
sentences.n: “und wenn sie noch so schwer ist” is a fixed concessive — however hard it may be. scheuen is to shy away from, to shrink from.

sentences.t: Die Alte ließ ihn ein, gab ihm Essen und Abends ein gutes Bett.
sentences.l: The old woman let him in, gave him food and in the evening a good bed.
sentences.n: einlassen is separable: ließ … ein. “Abends” is a genitive of time used as an adverb — of an evening, in the evening.

sentences.t: Am Morgen als er ausgeschlafen hatte, nahm die Alte einen Fingerhut von ihrem dürren Finger, reichte ihn dem Trommler hin,
sentences.l: In the morning when he had slept his fill, the old woman took a thimble from her withered finger, held it out to the drummer,
sentences.i: In the morning, when he had slept himself out, the old woman took a thimble from her withered finger, held it out to the drummer,
sentences.n: ausschlafen is to sleep as long as one needs — to sleep oneself out. der Fingerhut is literally a finger-hat: a thimble. hinreichen is separable: reichte … hin.

sentences.t: und sagte „jetzt geh an die Arbeit und schöpfe den Teich draußen mit diesem Fingerhut aus:
sentences.l: and said “now go to work and bale out the pond outside with this thimble:
sentences.i: and said “now set to work and empty the pond out there with this thimble:
sentences.n: ausschöpfen is separable, and its particle “aus” has been carried right to the end of the clause after “Fingerhut”. The impossible task with an absurd tool is the standard opening move of this kind of tale.

sentences.t: aber ehe es Nacht wird mußt du fertig sein, und alle Fische, die in dem Wasser sind, müssen nach ihrer Art und Größe ausgesucht und nebeneinander gelegt sein.“
sentences.l: but before it becomes night you must be finished, and all the fish that are in the water must be picked out and laid side by side according to their kind and size.”
sentences.i: but you must be finished before night falls, and all the fish that are in the water must be sorted out by kind and size and laid side by side.”
sentences.n: “nach ihrer Art und Größe” = according to their kind and size — Art here is species, not manner. “ausgesucht und … gelegt sein” is a passive built with sein rather than werden: must be in the state of having been sorted.

sentences.t: „Das ist eine seltsame Arbeit,“ sagte der Trommler, gieng aber zu dem Teich und fieng an zu schöpfen.
sentences.l: “That is a strange piece of work,” said the drummer, went nevertheless to the pond and began to bale.
sentences.i: “That is a strange piece of work,” said the drummer, but he went to the pond all the same and began to bale.
sentences.n: “aber” sits inside the clause here, after the verb, where English puts “but” at the front. schöpfen is to scoop or draw water.

sentences.t: Er schöpfte den ganzen Morgen, aber was kann man mit einem Fingerhut bei einem großen Wasser ausrichten, und wenn man tausend Jahre schöpft?
sentences.l: He baled the whole morning, but what can one accomplish with a thimble at a great water, even if one bales a thousand years?
sentences.i: He baled all morning — but what can anyone do with a thimble against a great body of water, though he bale a thousand years?
sentences.n: The narrator breaks into the present tense and asks the reader directly, a move this tale makes only twice. “und wenn” = even if. “ein großes Wasser” is a stretch of water, a body of water.

sentences.t: Als es Mittag war, dachte er „es ist alles umsonst, und ist einerlei ob ich arbeite oder nicht,“ hielt ein, und setzte sich nieder.
sentences.l: When it was midday, he thought “it is all for nothing, and it is all one whether I work or not,” stopped, and set himself down.
sentences.i: When midday came he thought “it is all for nothing, and it makes no difference whether I work or not”; he left off, and sat down.
sentences.n: “einerlei” = all one, all the same. einhalten is separable — hielt … ein, to leave off. sich niedersetzen is separable and reflexive: setzte sich nieder.

sentences.t: Da kam ein Mädchen aus dem Haus gegangen, stellte ihm ein Körbchen mit Essen hin, und sprach „du sitzest da so traurig, was fehlt dir?“
sentences.l: Then there came a girl walking out of the house, set down for him a little basket with food, and said “you are sitting there so sad, what ails you?”
sentences.i: Then a girl came walking out of the house, set a little basket of food down before him, and said “you sit there so sadly — what ails you?”
sentences.n: “kam … gegangen” — came gone — is the German way of joining motion to manner: came walking. hinstellen is separable: stellte … hin. “was fehlt dir?” is literally what is lacking to you, the standard German for what is the matter.

sentences.t: Er blickte es an und sah daß es wunderschön war.
sentences.l: He looked at it and saw that it was wonderfully beautiful.
sentences.i: He looked at her and saw that she was wonderfully beautiful.
sentences.n: das Mädchen is grammatically neuter, so German refers to the girl as “es” — it — all the way through this tale. The literal line keeps that; the idiomatic line puts it into English as “she”. This is grammar, not a comment on the girl.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte er, „ich kann die erste Arbeit nicht vollbringen, wie wird es mit den andern werden?
sentences.l: “Ah,” said he, “I cannot accomplish the first task, how will it be with the others?
sentences.i: “Ah,” said he, “I cannot get the first task done — how will it go with the others?
sentences.n: vollbringen is to bring to completion, accomplish. “wie wird es mit … werden” = how will it turn out with, what will become of.

sentences.t: Ich bin ausgegangen eine Königstochter zu suchen, die hier wohnen soll, aber ich habe sie nicht gefunden;
sentences.l: I have gone out to seek a king’s daughter who is said to live here, but I have not found her;
sentences.i: I set out to look for a king’s daughter who is supposed to live here, but I have not found her;
sentences.n: “die hier wohnen soll” — sollen used for hearsay: who is said to live here, who is supposed to. This is a common sense of sollen that has nothing to do with obligation.

sentences.t: ich will weiter gehen.“
sentences.l: I will go further on.”
sentences.i: I mean to go on my way.”
sentences.n: “weiter gehen” is printed as two words in 1857 where modern German writes weitergehen.

sentences.t: „Bleib hier,“ sagte das Mädchen, „ich will dir aus deiner Noth helfen.
sentences.l: “Stay here,” said the girl, “I will help you out of your distress.
sentences.i: “Stay here,” said the girl; “I will help you out of your trouble.
sentences.n: “Noth” is the 1857 spelling of Not — need, distress, a fix. helfen takes the dative: dir.

sentences.t: Du bist müde, lege deinen Kopf in meinen Schoos und schlaf.
sentences.l: You are tired, lay your head in my lap and sleep.
sentences.n: “Schoos” is the 1857 spelling of Schoß, the lap. Two plain imperatives, “lege” and “schlaf”, side by side.

sentences.t: Wenn du wieder aufwachst, so ist die Arbeit gethan.“
sentences.l: When you wake up again, then the work is done.”
sentences.n: “gethan” is the 1857 spelling of getan. The “so” at the head of the main clause simply answers the wenn-clause and need not be translated.

sentences.t: Der Trommler ließ sich das nicht zweimal sagen.
sentences.l: The drummer did not let himself be told that twice.
sentences.i: The drummer did not need to be told twice.
sentences.n: “sich etwas nicht zweimal sagen lassen” is a fixed idiom — not to need telling twice, to do a thing gladly and at once.

sentences.t: Sobald ihm die Augen zufielen, drehte sie einen Wunschring und sprach „Wasser herauf, Fische heraus.“
sentences.l: As soon as his eyes fell shut, she turned a wishing-ring and said “water up, fish out.”
sentences.i: As soon as his eyes closed, she turned a wishing-ring and said “water up, fish out.”
sentences.n: zufallen is separable: fielen … zu, of eyes falling shut. “ihm die Augen” is the dative of possession once more: his eyes. The ring’s four bare words are all the spell the tale gives.

sentences.t: Alsbald stieg das Wasser wie ein weißer Nebel in die Höhe und zog mit den andern Wolken fort,
sentences.l: At once the water rose like a white mist into the height and drew away with the other clouds,
sentences.i: At once the water rose like a white mist into the air and drifted off with the other clouds,
sentences.n: fortziehen is separable: zog … fort. “in die Höhe” = up into the air, a standard phrase. “die andern Wolken” — the other clouds — quietly makes the risen water one of them.

sentences.t: und die Fische schnalzten, sprangen ans Ufer, und legten sich nebeneinander, jeder nach seiner Größe und Art.
sentences.l: and the fish smacked, sprang onto the bank, and laid themselves side by side, each according to his size and kind.
sentences.i: and the fish flapped and smacked, sprang out onto the bank, and laid themselves side by side, each by its size and kind.
sentences.n: schnalzen is the smacking, snapping sound a fish makes out of water. “jeder nach seiner Größe und Art” answers the old woman’s demand word for word, which is how the tale shows the task exactly fulfilled.

sentences.t: Als der Trommler erwachte, sah er mit Erstaunen daß alles vollbracht war.
sentences.l: When the drummer awoke, he saw with astonishment that everything was accomplished.
sentences.n: “mit Erstaunen” = with astonishment. vollbringen appears here as the past participle vollbracht, matching the drummer’s own word for the task a few units earlier.

sentences.t: Aber das Mädchen sprach „einer von den Fischen liegt nicht bei seinesgleichen, sondern ganz allein.
sentences.l: But the girl said “one of the fish is not lying by his own kind, but quite alone.
sentences.i: But the girl said “one of the fish is not lying with its own kind, but quite by itself.
sentences.n: seinesgleichen — the like of him — is a fixed genitive form meaning one’s own kind. The girl’s instructions run for the next two sense-units and are the pattern for all three tasks.

sentences.t: Wenn die Alte heute Abend kommt, und sieht daß alles geschehen ist, was sie verlangt hat, so wird sie fragen „was soll dieser Fisch allein?“
sentences.l: When the old woman comes this evening, and sees that everything has happened that she demanded, then she will ask “what is this fish doing alone?”
sentences.i: When the old woman comes this evening and sees that all she demanded has been done, she will ask “what is this fish doing alone?”
sentences.n: “was soll dieser Fisch allein?” uses sollen with no main verb at all — what is this fish supposed to be, doing there alone. The 1857 printing opens a second quotation inside the first without closing the outer one, and the reader has to follow it by sense.

sentences.t: Dann wirf ihr den Fisch ins Angesicht und sprich „der soll für dich sein, alte Hexe.“
sentences.l: Then throw her the fish in the face and say “that one shall be for you, old witch.”
sentences.i: Then throw the fish in her face and say “that one is for you, old witch.”
sentences.n: “ins Angesicht” is the elevated word for face; the next sentence uses the everyday “Gesicht” for the same act. “ihr” is the dative of the person: in her face.

sentences.t: Abends kam die Alte, und als sie die Frage gethan hatte, so warf er ihr den Fisch ins Gesicht.
sentences.l: In the evening the old woman came, and when she had put the question, he threw her the fish in the face.
sentences.i: In the evening the old woman came, and when she had put the question, he threw the fish in her face.
sentences.n: “die Frage gethan” — done the question — where modern German says eine Frage stellen. The girl’s prediction is fulfilled to the letter, which the tale reports without comment.

sentences.t: Sie stellte sich als merkte sie es nicht und schwieg still, aber sie blickte ihn mit boshaften Augen an.
sentences.l: She acted as though she did not notice it and kept silent, but she looked at him with spiteful eyes.
sentences.i: She acted as though she had not noticed, and said nothing, but she looked at him with spiteful eyes.
sentences.n: “sich stellen als …” = to pretend, to act as if, with the subjunctive “merkte”. “schwieg still” is doubly emphatic: schweigen already means to be silent. anblicken is separable: blickte … an.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen sprach sie „gestern hast du es zu leicht gehabt, ich muß dir schwerere Arbeit geben.
sentences.l: On the next morning she said “yesterday you had it too easy, I must give you harder work.
sentences.i: Next morning she said “yesterday you had it too easy; I must set you harder work.
sentences.n: “leicht” here means easy, not light in weight. “am andern Morgen” = on the other morning, that is, the next morning — ander in 1857 German often simply means next.

sentences.t: Heute mußt du den ganzen Wald umhauen, das Holz in Scheite spalten und in Klaftern legen, und am Abend muß alles fertig sein.“
sentences.l: Today you must hew down the whole forest, split the wood into billets and lay it in cords, and in the evening everything must be finished.”
sentences.i: Today you must fell the whole forest, split the wood into billets and stack it in cords, and by evening it must all be done.”
sentences.n: umhauen is separable: to hew down, to fell. das Scheit is a split log of firewood; die Klafter is the old cord — a stacked measure of firewood roughly a fathom square. The second task is impossible on the same scale as the first.

sentences.t: Sie gab ihm eine Axt, einen Schläger und zwei Keile.
sentences.l: She gave him an axe, a beetle and two wedges.
sentences.i: She gave him an axe, a mallet and two wedges.
sentences.n: der Schläger here is the heavy wooden beetle or mallet that drives the wedges into a log; the wedges then split it. These are the right tools for the job, which is the point of the next sentence.

sentences.t: Aber die Axt war von Blei, der Schläger und die Keile waren von Blech.
sentences.l: But the axe was of lead, the beetle and the wedges were of tin plate.
sentences.i: But the axe was made of lead, and the mallet and the wedges of tin plate.
sentences.n: das Blech is thin sheet metal, tin plate — soft and useless for splitting. The trick is that the tools are correct in shape and worthless in substance.

sentences.t: Als er anfieng zu hauen, so legte sich die Axt um, und Schläger und Keile drückten sich zusammen.
sentences.l: When he began to hew, the axe bent over, and beetle and wedges pressed themselves together.
sentences.i: When he set to hewing, the axe bent over, and the mallet and wedges crumpled up.
sentences.n: “legte sich … um” is umlegen used reflexively — laid itself over, that is, bent double. sich zusammendrücken is to be squashed together.

sentences.t: Er wußte sich nicht zu helfen, aber Mittags kam das Mädchen wieder mit dem Essen und tröstete ihn.
sentences.l: He did not know how to help himself, but at midday the girl came again with the food and comforted him.
sentences.i: He was at a loss what to do, but at midday the girl came again with the food and comforted him.
sentences.n: “sich nicht zu helfen wissen” returns from earlier in the block — the tale’s standing phrase for being helpless. “Mittags” is another adverbial genitive of time.

sentences.t: „Lege deinen Kopf in meinen Schoos,“ sagte sie, „und schlaf, wenn du aufwachst, so ist die Arbeit gethan.“
sentences.l: “Lay your head in my lap,” said she, “and sleep, when you wake up, then the work is done.”
sentences.i: “Lay your head in my lap,” said she, “and sleep; when you wake, the work will be done.”
sentences.n: The girl repeats her own words from the first task almost exactly, and the tale repeats them with her — a fixed formula, not carelessness.

sentences.t: Sie drehte ihren Wunschring, in dem Augenblick sank der ganze Wald mit Krachen zusammen,
sentences.l: She turned her wishing-ring, in that moment the whole forest sank down with a crashing,
sentences.i: She turned her wishing-ring, and in that instant the whole forest came crashing down,
sentences.n: zusammensinken is separable: sank … zusammen. “mit Krachen” uses the infinitive as a noun — with a cracking, with a crash; German makes nouns out of infinitives freely.

sentences.t: das Holz spaltete sich von selbst, und legte sich in Klaftern zusammen;
sentences.l: the wood split itself of its own accord, and laid itself together in cords;
sentences.i: the wood split of its own accord and stacked itself in cords;
sentences.n: “von selbst” = by itself, of its own accord. Both verbs are reflexive, which is German’s usual way of saying a thing happens without an agent — English uses the plain intransitive.

sentences.t: es war als ob unsichtbare Riesen die Arbeit vollbrächten.
sentences.l: it was as though invisible giants were accomplishing the work.
sentences.n: “als ob” takes the subjunctive “vollbrächten” — as if they were. The giants are a simile only; the real giants of this tale were left behind at the foot of the mountain.

sentences.t: Als er aufwachte, sagte das Mädchen „siehst du das Holz ist geklaftert und gelegt:
sentences.l: When he awoke, the girl said “you see the wood is corded and stacked:
sentences.i: When he awoke, the girl said “you see, the wood is corded and stacked:
sentences.n: “geklaftert” is a verb made from die Klafter — to lay wood up in cords. “siehst du” runs straight into the next clause without a comma, as the printing has it.

sentences.t: nur ein einziger Ast ist übrig, aber wenn die Alte heute Abend kommt und fragt was der Ast solle,
sentences.l: only a single branch is left over, but when the old woman comes this evening and asks what the branch is for,
sentences.i: only one single branch is left; but when the old woman comes this evening and asks what that branch is doing there,
sentences.n: “was der Ast solle” is sollen again with no main verb — what the branch is supposed to be. “solle” is subjunctive because it sits inside the reported question.

sentences.t: so gib ihr damit einen Schlag und sprich „der soll für dich sein, du Hexe.“
sentences.l: then give her a blow with it and say “that one shall be for you, you witch.”
sentences.i: then give her a blow with it and say “that one is for you, you witch.”
sentences.n: The formula matches the fish exactly, with only “alte Hexe” shortened to “du Hexe” — the tale builds its three tasks out of repeated wording with small variations.

sentences.t: Die Alte kam, „siehst du,“ sprach sie, „wie leicht die Arbeit war: aber für wen liegt der Ast noch da?“
sentences.l: The old woman came, “you see,” said she, “how easy the work was: but for whom is the branch still lying there?”
sentences.i: The old woman came. “You see,” said she, “how easy the work was — but who is that branch lying there for?”
sentences.n: She asks the question the girl foretold, but phrases it herself as “für wen”, for whom — walking straight into the answer she is about to get.

sentences.t: „Für dich, du Hexe“ antwortete er und gab ihr einen Schlag damit.
sentences.l: “For you, you witch” answered he and gave her a blow with it.
sentences.i: “For you, you witch,” he answered, and struck her with it.
sentences.n: “damit” = with that, with it — da(r)- plus a preposition, standing for a thing rather than a person.

sentences.t: Aber sie that als fühlte sie es nicht,
sentences.l: But she acted as though she did not feel it,
sentences.i: But she acted as though she felt nothing,
sentences.n: The same “that als …” construction as with the fish, and the same result. “that” is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun (modern tun).

sentences.t: lachte höhnisch und sprach „Morgen früh sollst du alles Holz auf einen Haufen legen, es anzünden und verbrennen.“
sentences.l: laughed scornfully and said “tomorrow morning you shall lay all the wood on a heap, set light to it and burn it.”
sentences.i: laughed scornfully and said “tomorrow morning you shall pile all the wood in one heap, set light to it and burn it up.”
sentences.n: anzünden is separable — to kindle, set alight. The third task undoes the second: the wood he has just corded is to be burnt.

sentences.t: Er stand mit Anbruch des Tages auf und fieng an das Holz herbei zu holen,
sentences.l: He got up at break of day and began to fetch the wood over,
sentences.i: He rose at daybreak and set about carrying the wood together,
sentences.n: aufstehen is separable and its halves stand far apart: stand … auf. “herbei zu holen” is printed as three words in 1857 where modern German writes herbeizuholen.

sentences.t: aber wie kann ein einziger Mensch einen ganzen Wald zusammen tragen?
sentences.l: but how can a single person carry a whole forest together?
sentences.i: but how can one man alone carry a whole forest together?
sentences.n: The narrator addresses the reader in the present tense for the second and last time in this block, exactly as at the thimble. “zusammen tragen” is two words in 1857 for zusammentragen.

sentences.t: die Arbeit rückte nicht fort.
sentences.l: the work did not move forward.
sentences.i: the work made no headway.
sentences.n: fortrücken is separable: rückte … fort, to move forward, to make progress. The 1857 printing begins this clause with a small letter after the question mark, and the sense-unit keeps that.

sentences.t: Doch das Mädchen verließ ihn nicht in der Noth: es brachte ihm Mittags seine Speise,
sentences.l: Yet the girl did not leave him in his distress: it brought him his food at midday,
sentences.i: Yet the girl did not fail him in his distress: she brought him his food at midday,
sentences.n: “es” is the girl again — das Mädchen is neuter. verlassen with a person means to abandon, not merely to leave a place.

sentences.t: und als er gegessen hatte, legte er seinen Kopf in den Schoos und schlief ein.
sentences.l: and when he had eaten, he laid his head in the lap and fell asleep.
sentences.i: and when he had eaten, he laid his head in her lap and fell asleep.
sentences.n: German writes only “in den Schoos”, in the lap, where English needs a possessive — with parts of the body and the like, German leaves the owner to be understood. einschlafen is separable: schlief … ein.

sentences.t: Bei seinem Erwachen brannte der ganze Holzstoß in einer ungeheuern Flamme, die ihre Zungen bis in den Himmel ausstreckte.
sentences.l: At his awaking the whole woodpile was burning in an enormous flame, which stretched out its tongues right up into the sky.
sentences.i: When he awoke, the whole woodpile was burning in one enormous flame that stretched its tongues right up into the sky.
sentences.n: “bei seinem Erwachen” turns the verb erwachen into a noun — at his awaking. ausstrecken is separable: streckte … aus. The tongues of flame are the same picture in German as in English.

sentences.t: „Hör mich an,“ sprach das Mädchen, „wenn die Hexe kommt, wird sie dir allerlei auftragen:
sentences.l: “Hear me,” said the girl, “when the witch comes, she will charge you with all manner of things:
sentences.i: “Listen to me,” said the girl. “When the witch comes she will set you all sorts of orders:
sentences.n: anhören is separable: hör … an. This is the first time the tale calls the old woman “die Hexe” outright in the girl’s mouth. auftragen is to charge someone with a task.

sentences.t: thust du ohne Furcht was sie verlangt, so kann sie dir nichts anhaben:
sentences.l: if you do without fear what she demands, then she can do you no harm:
sentences.i: if you do what she demands without fear, she can do you no harm:
sentences.n: “thust du …” has no wenn: German makes a conditional simply by putting the verb first, and the “so” answers it. “jemandem nichts anhaben können” is the fixed phrase for being unable to harm someone.

sentences.t: fürchtest du dich aber, so packt dich das Feuer und verzehrt dich.
sentences.l: but if you are afraid, then the fire seizes you and consumes you.
sentences.i: but if you are afraid, the fire will seize you and devour you.
sentences.n: The same verb-first conditional again, in the opposite case, so that the two halves stand as a matched pair. The present tense carries a future sense, as it often does in German.

sentences.t: Zuletzt, wenn du alles gethan hast, so packe sie mit beiden Händen, und wirf sie mitten in die Glut.“
sentences.l: At the last, when you have done everything, then seize her with both hands, and throw her into the middle of the blaze.”
sentences.i: At the last, when you have done it all, seize her with both hands and throw her into the middle of the blaze.”
sentences.n: “packe” and “wirf” are imperatives. die Glut is the glowing heart of a fire, hotter than die Flamme. The girl’s instruction is plain and the tale does not soften what it asks for.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen gieng fort, und die Alte kam herangeschlichen,
sentences.l: The girl went away, and the old woman came creeping up,
sentences.i: The girl went off, and the old woman came creeping up,
sentences.n: fortgehen is separable: gieng … fort. heranschleichen is to sneak or creep up on someone — a verb chosen for her.

sentences.t: „hu! mich friert,“ sagte sie,
sentences.l: “ugh! I am cold,” said she,
sentences.i: “ugh! I am freezing,” said she,
sentences.n: “mich friert” is impersonal — it freezes me — with the person in the accusative and no subject at all. Modern German more often says mir ist kalt or ich friere.

sentences.t: „aber das ist ein Feuer, das brennt, das wärmt mir die alten Knochen, da wird mir wohl.
sentences.l: “but that is a fire, that burns, that warms my old bones for me, there I feel well.
sentences.i: “but there is a fire that burns! that warms my old bones — this does me good.
sentences.n: “das wärmt mir die alten Knochen” is the dative of possession yet again: warms the old bones for me, that is, my old bones. “da wird mir wohl” is impersonal — it becomes well to me.

sentences.t: Aber dort liegt ein Klotz, der will nicht brennen, den hol mir heraus.
sentences.l: But there lies a block, it will not burn, fetch it out for me.
sentences.i: But there lies a log that will not burn — fetch it out for me.
sentences.n: “der will nicht brennen” uses wollen of a thing: it refuses to, it will not. herausholen is separable, and the imperative “hol” drops its final e as speech does.

sentences.t: Hast du das noch gethan, so bist du frei, und kannst ziehen wohin du willst.
sentences.l: Have you done that too, then you are free, and can go wherever you want.
sentences.i: Once you have done that as well, you are free, and may go wherever you please.
sentences.n: Another verb-first conditional with no wenn: have you done that, then … ziehen of a person means to travel, to move on.

sentences.t: Nur munter hinein.“
sentences.l: Only briskly in.”
sentences.i: In with you, and briskly.”
sentences.n: Three words, no verb, no mercy — she is telling him to jump into the fire. “munter” is brisk, lively; “hinein” carries the direction, in and away from the speaker.

sentences.t: Der Trommler besann sich nicht lange, sprang mitten in die Flammen,
sentences.l: The drummer did not reflect long, sprang into the middle of the flames,
sentences.i: The drummer did not stop to think, but sprang into the middle of the flames,
sentences.n: sich besinnen is to think a thing over, to reflect. The tale reports his obedience with no comment on his courage, exactly as the girl’s instruction had it.

sentences.t: aber sie thaten ihm nichts, nicht einmal die Haare konnten sie ihm versengen.
sentences.l: but they did nothing to him, not even the hairs could they singe for him.
sentences.i: but they did him no harm — they could not so much as singe his hair.
sentences.n: “thaten” is the 1857 spelling of taten, from thun. “konnten sie ihm versengen” is the dative of possession one final time: could singe the hairs for him, that is, his hair. The verb comes first in the clause because “nicht einmal die Haare” has taken the front position.

sentences.t: Er trug den Klotz heraus und legte ihn hin.
sentences.l: He carried the block out and laid it down.
sentences.n: heraustragen and hinlegen are both separable: trug … heraus, legte … hin. Two flat little actions before the transformation.

sentences.t: Kaum aber hatte das Holz die Erde berührt, so verwandelte es sich,
sentences.l: But scarcely had the wood touched the ground, when it transformed itself,
sentences.i: But scarcely had the wood touched the ground when it was transformed,
sentences.n: “kaum … hatte, so …” is the German pair for scarcely had … when. sich verwandeln is reflexive where English uses a passive: it changed itself, it was transformed.

sentences.t: und das schöne Mädchen stand vor ihm, das ihm in der Noth geholfen hatte:
sentences.l: and the beautiful girl stood before him, that had helped him in his distress:
sentences.i: and there stood the beautiful girl before him who had helped him in his distress:
sentences.n: The relative clause has been pushed past the verb to the end of the sentence — the girl first, then the identification. “das” is the neuter relative, because das Mädchen is neuter.

sentences.t: und an den seidenen goldglänzenden Kleidern, die es anhatte, merkte er wohl daß es die Königstochter war.
sentences.l: and by the silken, gold-gleaming garments that it had on, he well perceived that it was the king’s daughter.
sentences.i: and by the silken, gold-gleaming garments she was wearing he saw plainly that she was the king’s daughter.
sentences.n: anhaben is separable: to have on, to wear. “merkte er wohl” — wohl here is not “well” of manner but an intensifier: he saw plainly, he perceived clearly. The tale never troubles to explain how the girl who fed him and the log in the fire were the same person.

sentences.t: Aber die Alte lachte giftig und sprach „du meinst du hättest sie, aber du hast sie noch nicht.“
sentences.l: But the old woman laughed venomously and said “you think you had her, but you do not have her yet.”
sentences.i: But the old woman laughed venomously and said “you think you have her, but you have not got her yet.”
sentences.n: “du hättest sie” is subjunctive inside the reported thought — you think you have her. giftig is literally poisonous, used of a laugh as English uses “venomous”.

sentences.t: Eben wollte sie auf das Mädchen losgehen, und es fortziehen,
sentences.l: Just then she was about to go at the girl, and drag it away,
sentences.i: She was on the point of setting upon the girl and dragging her off,
sentences.n: “eben wollte sie” = she was just about to. losgehen auf is to go at, to set upon someone. fortziehen is separable: to drag away.

sentences.t: da packte er die Alte mit beiden Händen, hob sie in die Höhe,
sentences.l: when he seized the old woman with both hands, lifted her up into the air,
sentences.i: when he seized the old woman with both hands, heaved her up,
sentences.n: “da” at the head of the main clause here means when, whereupon — the turn of the action. The drummer does exactly what the girl told him to do, in her words.

sentences.t: und warf sie den Flammen in den Rachen, die über ihr zusammenschlugen, als freuten sie sich daß sie eine Hexe verzehren sollten.
sentences.l: and threw her to the flames into the maw, which closed together over her, as though they rejoiced that they should consume a witch.
sentences.i: and threw her into the maw of the flames, which closed together over her as though they were glad to be devouring a witch.
sentences.n: “warf sie den Flammen in den Rachen” splits what English joins: threw her to the flames, into the maw. der Rachen is the gullet of a beast, so the fire is a devouring animal. “als freuten sie sich” is the subjunctive of comparison with no als ob — German can drop the ob and put the verb first instead. The tale does not soften the killing.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter blickte darauf den Trommler an,
sentences.l: The king’s daughter thereupon looked at the drummer,
sentences.i: The king’s daughter then looked at the drummer,
sentences.n: anblicken is separable, and the particle “an” waits until the end of the clause. “darauf” = thereupon, after that.

sentences.t: und als sie sah daß es ein schöner Jüngling war und bedachte daß er sein Leben daran gesetzt hatte, um sie zu erlösen,
sentences.l: and when she saw that he was a handsome youth and considered that he had staked his life on it, in order to redeem her,
sentences.i: and when she saw that he was a handsome young man, and thought how he had staked his life to set her free,
sentences.n: “sein Leben daran gesetzt” — to set one’s life on it, to stake it. “um … zu erlösen” is the purpose infinitive: in order to. erlösen is the standing word in these tales for releasing someone from a spell.

sentences.t: so reichte sie ihm die Hand und sprach „du hast alles für mich gewagt, aber ich will auch für dich alles thun.
sentences.l: she reached him her hand and said “you have risked everything for me, but I too will do everything for you.
sentences.i: she gave him her hand and said “you have risked everything for me, and I in turn will do everything for you.
sentences.n: “so” opens the main clause after the long when-clause and simply answers it. “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Versprichst du mir deine Treue, so sollst du mein Gemahl werden.
sentences.l: If you promise me your faith, then you shall be my husband.
sentences.i: If you pledge me your troth, you shall be my husband.
sentences.n: “Versprichst du mir …” is a conditional with no wenn — German makes one by putting the verb first. die Treue is the noun, faith or fidelity pledged; it returns in the song. der Gemahl is the elevated word for a husband.

sentences.t: An Reichthümern fehlt es uns nicht, wir haben genug an dem, was die Hexe hier zusammen getragen hat.“
sentences.l: Of riches there is no lack to us, we have enough of what the witch has gathered together here.”
sentences.i: We shall want for nothing: we have enough of what the witch gathered together here.”
sentences.n: “es fehlt uns nicht an …” is impersonal — there is no lack to us. “Reichthümern” is the 1857 spelling of Reichtümern. “zusammen getragen” is two words for what modern German writes as zusammengetragen.

sentences.t: Sie führte ihn in das Haus, da standen Kisten und Kasten, die mit ihren Schätzen angefüllt waren.
sentences.l: She led him into the house, there stood chests and boxes which were filled with her treasures.
sentences.i: She led him into the house, where chests and coffers stood filled with her treasures.
sentences.n: “Kisten und Kasten” is a set pairing, much like English “boxes and chests” — the two words are nearly synonymous and travel together. “ihren” is the witch’s, not the princess’s.

sentences.t: Sie ließen Gold und Silber liegen und nahmen nur die Edelsteine.
sentences.l: They let gold and silver lie and took only the precious stones.
sentences.i: They left the gold and silver where they lay and took only the jewels.
sentences.n: “liegen lassen” — to let lie, to leave behind. The choice is practical: jewels carry more value in less weight.

sentences.t: Sie wollte nicht länger auf dem Glasberg bleiben,
sentences.l: She did not want to stay on the glass mountain any longer,
sentences.n: “nicht länger” = no longer, not any more; länger is the comparative of lang.

sentences.t: da sprach er zu ihr „setze dich zu mir auf meinen Sattel, so fliegen wir hinab wie Vögel.“
sentences.l: then he said to her “seat yourself beside me on my saddle, then we fly down like birds.”
sentences.i: so he said to her “sit beside me on my saddle, and we shall fly down like birds.”
sentences.n: “da” here is the narrative then, whereupon. The present “fliegen wir” carries a future sense, as German so often does.

sentences.t: „Der alte Sattel gefällt mir nicht,“ sagte sie, „ich brauche nur an meinem Wunschring zu drehen, so sind wir zu Haus.“
sentences.l: “The old saddle does not please me,” said she, “I need only turn my wishing-ring, then we are at home.”
sentences.i: “I do not care for the old saddle,” said she; “I need only turn my wishing-ring and we are home.”
sentences.n: gefallen is the standard German frame for liking something: the thing pleases the person, who stands in the dative. “an … drehen” is to turn something round, with an where English uses no preposition at all.

sentences.t: „Wohlan,“ antwortete der Trommler, „so wünsch uns vor das Stadtthor.“
sentences.l: “Well then,” answered the drummer, “so wish us before the town gate.”
sentences.i: “Very well,” answered the drummer, “then wish us to the town gate.”
sentences.n: “wohlan” is an old exclamation of assent — well then, come now. “Stadtthor” is the 1857 spelling of Stadttor.

sentences.t: Im Nu waren sie dort,
sentences.l: In an instant they were there,
sentences.n: “im Nu” is a fixed phrase — in an instant. der Nu is a noun here, and has nothing to do with the adverb nun, now.

sentences.t: der Trommler aber sprach „ich will erst zu meinen Eltern gehen und ihnen Nachricht geben, harre mein hier auf dem Feld, ich will bald zurück sein.“
sentences.l: but the drummer said “I will go first to my parents and give them news, wait for me here on the field, I will soon be back.”
sentences.i: but the drummer said “I will go to my parents first and give them the news; wait for me here in the field, I shall soon be back.”
sentences.n: “harre mein” — harren takes the genitive, “mein” being the old genitive of ich: wait for me. It is a deliberately elevated word; the everyday one is warte auf mich.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte die Königstochter, „ich bitte dich, nimm dich in Acht,
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the king’s daughter, “I beg you, take yourself in care,
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the king’s daughter, “I beg you, take care,
sentences.n: “sich in Acht nehmen” is the fixed phrase for taking care, being on one’s guard. die Acht here is heed, not the number eight.

sentences.t: küsse deine Eltern bei deiner Ankunft nicht auf die rechte Wange,
sentences.l: do not kiss your parents on the right cheek at your arrival,
sentences.i: do not kiss your parents on the right cheek when you arrive,
sentences.n: “bei deiner Ankunft” = at your arrival. The prohibition is arbitrary and the tale offers no reason for it — this is simply the rule the story runs on, and it is stated once, plainly, and then broken.

sentences.t: denn sonst wirst du alles vergessen, und ich bleibe hier allein und verlassen auf dem Feld zurück.“
sentences.l: for otherwise you will forget everything, and I stay behind here alone and forsaken on the field.”
sentences.i: for otherwise you will forget everything, and I shall be left here alone and forsaken in the field.”
sentences.n: zurückbleiben is separable and its particle “zurück” has travelled to the end of the sentence, well clear of “bleibe”. The present “ich bleibe” again carries a future sense.

sentences.t: „Wie kann ich dich vergessen?“ sagte er und versprach ihr in die Hand recht bald wieder zu kommen.
sentences.l: “How can I forget you?” said he and promised her into the hand to come again right soon.
sentences.i: “How could I forget you?” said he, and gave her his hand on it that he would come back very soon.
sentences.n: “versprach ihr in die Hand” — promised into her hand — is the gesture of striking a bargain by hand, the old form of a binding promise. “recht bald” = right soon, very soon.

sentences.t: Als er in sein väterliches Haus trat, wußte niemand wer er war,
sentences.l: When he stepped into his father’s house, nobody knew who he was,
sentences.i: When he stepped into his father’s house, nobody knew who he was,
sentences.n: “väterlich” is the adjective from Vater — the paternal house, his father’s house. “trat” is the past of treten.

sentences.t: so hatte er sich verändert, denn die drei Tage, die er auf dem Glasberg zugebracht hatte, waren drei lange Jahre gewesen.
sentences.l: so had he changed himself, for the three days that he had spent on the glass mountain had been three long years.
sentences.i: so much had he changed; for the three days he had spent on the glass mountain had been three long years.
sentences.n: “so hatte er sich verändert” with the verb before the subject means so much had he changed — a result clause. The passing of time on the enchanted mountain is stated flatly and never explained.
